query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (HEA) with density below 6 g/cm³, the metastable microstructure featuring a mixed solid solution with intermetallic compounds facilitates localized Mg segregation during thermal exposure. This segregation promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, MgO-rich surface layer during high-temperature oxidation, which enhances oxidation resistance; however, the same compositional gradients simultaneously establish microgalvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or rapidly solidified HEA with a non-equilibrium microstructure comprising a solid-solution matrix and dispersed metastable intermetallic compounds containing Mg.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to sustained high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 700–900 °C in air) and to controlled corrosive environments (e.g., NaCl aqueous solution) in a side-by-side, unnamed controlled comparison.
generation.conditions: All tests are conducted under conditions where the alloy density remains below 6 g/cm³, temperatures are maintained below incipient melting, and exposure durations allow significant diffusion of Mg to occur (e.g., several hours at high temperature) or initiate localized corrosion in the aqueous environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of micron-scale Mg-rich regions and their subsequent oxidation to form a dense MgO surface layer mediate the changes in oxidation and corrosion behavior.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to high temperatures, metastable phases promote Mg diffusion and segregation toward the surface. The segregated Mg reacts with oxygen to form a continuous MgO-rich scale that effectively passivates the surface during oxidation. In contrast, under corrosive conditions the spatial heterogeneity in Mg content creates compositional gradients that serve as microgalvanic couples, locally intensifying corrosion where the protective oxide is incomplete or disrupted.
generation.predicted_outcome: After high-temperature oxidation, the alloy is predicted to display a uniform, adherent MgO-rich scale with improved oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state, whereas under corrosive attack, regions with pronounced Mg segregation will exhibit higher localized corrosion rates compared to the initial non-equilibrium baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial as-cast non-equilibrium microstructure prior to thermal treatment or controlled corrosion exposure serves as the baseline.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for Mg-containing HEAs engineered with density below 6 g/cm³ and must be tested within temperature ranges that avoid incipient melting yet allow significant Mg diffusion, as well as in corrosive environments that are sufficiently aggressive to reveal galvanic effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Mg diffusion and oxide scale formation, as well as the magnitude of the galvanic driving forces under corrosive conditions, are not precisely quantified and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples exhibiting the non-equilibrium microstructure. One set is subjected to prolonged high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 750 °C for 5 hours in air) while the other is maintained as-cast. In parallel, both sets are exposed separately to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) for equivalent times. Microstructural evolution will be characterized by SEM/EDS and XRD, and surface oxide formation will be evaluated via XPS. Corrosion rates will be measured by electrochemical methods (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Surface oxide layer continuity and composition (via SEM/EDS, XPS)
Microstructure and phase distribution (via XRD, TEM)
Weight loss or thickness changes after oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature treatment does not lead to the formation of a continuous MgO-rich surface layer and if no significant increase in localized corrosion rates is observed in the regions with Mg segregation compared to the as-cast baseline, then the proposed mechanism of Mg segregation driving dual effects on oxidation and corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One promising design strategy involves the development of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), which incorporate multiple elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios to achieve property combinations beyond those achievable in conventional binary or ternary systems. While this concept has been widely explored in high-entropy alloys, its application to Mg-rich systems remains limited and may offer new pathways for improving corrosion resistance, mechanical performance, and maintaining a low density. While prior studies have investigated Mg-Ti, Mg-Zn, and Zn-Ti binary alloys individually, the combined effects of Ti and Zn in bulk Mg-rich multi-element systems remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to phase stability, passivation behavior, and mechanical properties.

Several studies have explored Mg-Zn, Mg-Ti, and Zn-Ti alloys for their potential to improve corrosion resistance and mechanical performance [,,,,]. Mg-Zn alloys have been shown to promote grain refinement and ZnO-rich surface films, with corrosion current densities (icorr) typically ranging from 10 to 100 µA/cm2 in NaCl solutions, although their poor hardness (less than ~1 GPa) limits their broader implementation []. Ti additions to Mg offer excellent corrosion resistance, often reducing icorr to the range of 1–10 µA/cm2, but are hindered by poor solubility in Mg and higher cost [,]. However, sputtered Mg-Ti films have demonstrated passivation via TiO2-rich layers and reduced current densities, although this line of study lacks bulk validation []. Binary Zn-Ti alloys have shown promising corrosion resistance (e.g., ~2 µA/cm2) and improved surface passivation due to Ti rich phases, but still face challenges in balancing degradation rate with mechanical robustness []. Recent work by Mukhtar et al. demonstrated that mechanical alloying followed by compaction and sintering can successfully produce bulk Mg-Ti-Zn alloys with refined nanostructures and enhanced mechanical properties []. Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures. Physicochemical, microstructural, and mechanical characterization was performed for the selected alloy compositions.
